why_faster: Not stated by the suite. caveats: Compares the stable Rust sort against C++ std::sort (unstable), so the algorithms differ by design. name: D dmd compile throughput (nordlow/compiler-benchmark) vs clang, gcc, clang++ and g++
baseline: clang 23.1.1, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1 (C) and clang++ 23.1.1, g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1 (C++) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) a single massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function for check, compile and Total=Build+Run, untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: D (dmd 2.113.0) Total=Build+Run 13 us/f untemplated (19 templated), compile 10.3 us/f, vs C (clang 23.1.1) 118 us/f, C++ (clang++ 23.1.1) 236 us/f (107 templated), C++ (g++-15) 303 us/f (600 templated), C (gcc-15) 392 us/f. About 9x faster than clang C and 23x faster than g++-15 untemplated (derived from page data). The README states 6x-38x. LLVM-based ldmd2 is 95 us/f and GCC-based gdc is 527 us/f, so the speed comes from dmd's own backend.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler versions listed in the README table (dmd 2.113.0-95551bb, ldmd2 1.43.0, gdc 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1, gcc 15.3.0, g++ 15.3.0, gcc 16.2.1); optimization flags are not stated in the README, which describes the test as 'unoptimized code-generation scaling'.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
why_faster: README: dmd's custom backend and front end do little optimization work; comparing dmd with LLVM-based ldmd2 and GCC-based gdc on the same D source isolates backend cost (dmd about 6x faster than ldmd2 and about 38x faster than gdc).
tradeoffs: dmd generates less optimized code than LDC or GCC; this claim is about build time, not run time. In the README's table Zig (110 us/f) is on par with clang C (118) and Odin (147), C3 (153) and Rust (187) are slower than dmd but not faster than clang, so only dmd is a clear compile-time win.
caveats: Synthetic arithmetic call chains with no header parsing, standard-library or module resolution; the README says it does not reflect real builds. Baseline is not -O3: C and C++ flags are not documented, so the optimization levels are unmatched and the claim is a compile-time comparison, not the usual run-time one. The README prose and tables disagree slightly (11.5 vs 10.3 us/f). The repository's benchmark script (named 'benchmark') was not opened; the raw URL for 'benchmark.py' returned 404 and the plain 'benchmark' fetch returned a 6-byte body, so flags could not be read.

name: Rust regex crate in mariomka/regex-benchmark vs C PCRE2, C++ Boost.Regex and C++ std::regex
baseline: PCRE2 10.36 (C), Boost.Regex 1.65 (C++) and libstdc++ std::regex (C++, g++ 7.5.0)
workload: Count non-overlapping matches of three patterns (e-mail, URI, IPv4) over a concatenation of the Learn X in Y minutes docs repository; timing includes pattern compilation.
claimed_speedup: Rust 'Original' total 57.63 ms (email 26.66, URI 25.70, IP 5.28) vs C PCRE2 251.37 ms, C++ Boost 104.23 ms, C++ STL 1023.49 ms; community 'Optimized' rows: Rust 27.94 ms vs C PCRE2 87.87 ms, C++ Boost 104.28 ms, C++ STL 1021.10 ms. About 4.4x faster than PCRE2 as submitted and 3.1x in the optimized rows (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.5.0 and PCRE2 10.36-2 (C), g++ 7.5.0 and Boost 1.65.1.0 (C++), rustc 1.51.0 and regex 1.4.5 (Rust), via Docker image mariomka/regex-benchmark:1.6; compiler flags are not stated in the README.
hardware: MacBook Pro (16-inch, 2019), 2.4 GHz Intel Core i9, 32 GB, macOS Big Sur 11.2.3 (Docker image run on this machine)
tradeoffs: The regex crate has no backreferences or lookaround and guarantees linear-time matching.
caveats: Toolchains are from 2021 (rustc 1.51, gcc 7.5, PCRE2 10.36) and the benchmark repo is archived (last commit 2021-10-18; archived 2026-01-28), so current PCRE2 JIT or Rust results may differ. The README notes the input 'isn't the best representative text'. It is not clear that the C PCRE2 'Original' row uses the JIT; the optimized row is about 3x faster. The benchmark repo's page does not show Zig. The same repo's nim-regex row is already catalogued. The mechanism is not stated by the benchmark. The rebar barometer from another search is the stronger evidence for the regex crate.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): WebSearch for cross-language regex shootouts; github.com/mariomka/regex-benchmark README (also the source of the catalogued nim-regex row)

name: mosdepth (Nim) vs samtools depth and bedtools genomecov
baseline: samtools depth (C, htslib pileup) and bedtools genomecov (C++); sambamba depth (D) also compared
workload: Per-base depth of coverage for a 30X human genome in BAM and CRAM input, with 1 or 3 decompression threads, plus window mode.
claimed_speedup: README: 'per-base depth about 2x as fast samtools depth'. Table (30X genome, BAM, 1 thread, per-base): mosdepth 25:23 (1.00), samtools 50:12 (1.98x slower), bedtools 2:14:44 (5.31x slower), sambamba 2:24:53 (5.71x slower); CRAM: samtools 1.79x slower. mosdepth with 3 threads 14:27 (0.57) in BAM. Memory: mosdepth 1196 MB vs samtools 27 MB and bedtools 1908 MB.
why_faster: README 'how it works': mosdepth keeps one array per chromosome, increments at each read start and decrements at each stop and takes a cumulative sum, with no per-read or per-base tracking objects; samtools depth uses its pileup machinery that tracks each read and each base. The README notes the cost: memory about 32 bits times the longest chromosome (1 GB for chr1).
tradeoffs: Uses far more memory than samtools depth (1196 MB vs 27 MB); slower for small one-off regional queries; relies on htslib (C) through the hts-nim wrapper for BAM/CRAM decoding.
caveats: First-party README table with no hardware, compiler or flags stated. The README cites a Bioinformatics article (doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btx699) that was not opened (journal sites are blocked here); if its table matches, tier B applies. This is an algorithm win rather than a language win, since the decoding is htslib C code; the speedup comes from the difference-array method. The README also reports no differences in output versus samtools depth defaults when overlap detection is off. Baseline is not an -O3 compile of the same algorithm.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): Nim and D bioinformatics tools that beat C/C++ tools; github.com/brentp/mosdepth README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Sambamba (D) vs samtools
baseline: samtools 1.4 (C, htslib): flagstat, index, markdup, view and sort on BAM files
workload: SAM/BAM processing: flagstat, index, markdup, view and sort, as compared in the third-party sambamBench-nf pipeline run on a 16-CPU, 120 GB node at CRG (per the sambamba README).
claimed_speedup: README: flagstat 1.4x faster than samtools, index similar, markdup almost 6x faster, view 4x faster; sort is where samtools wins, though Sambamba is up to 2x faster on large-RAM machines (120GB+).
compiler_and_flags: Sambamba built with LDC (README example LDC 1.32.0 / DMD v2.102.2 / LLVM 14.0.6); samtools build and flags for the comparison not stated.
hardware: Probably a single node with 16 CPUs and 120 GB memory at CRG (the sample run described in the README of guigolab/sambamBench-nf; that this is the run behind the quoted numbers is unverified). Sambamba's own timing file in the repo (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/biod/sambamba/HEAD/test/benchmark/stats.org) lists an AMD Ryzen 7 3700X but only times sambamba itself.
why_faster: README: Sambamba's original advantage over samtools was parallelized BAM reading and writing (started 2012); samtools 1.4 (March 2017) 'reached some parity'.
stars_or_usage: 613 stars; README says over 1000 citations and over 250,000 Conda installs
tradeoffs: Multithreaded design; some older Intel Xeons segfault under heavy hyper-threading per the README; sort loses to samtools on ordinary machines.
caveats: Numbers are the README's summary of an external report (public-docs.crg.es sambamba_ws_report.html) that could not be opened (host blocked), and the sambamBench-nf README gives no figures. The comparison is with samtools 1.4 from 2017; current samtools may differ, and thread counts are not stated. A peer-reviewed article exists (Tarasov et al., Bioinformatics 2015, doi 10.1093/bioinformatics/btv098) but was not opened. README license text reads GPLv2+. Most of the speedup is parallelism rather than the language.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): Nim and D bioinformatics tools that beat C/C++ tools; github.com/biod/sambamba README and test/benchmark/stats.org opened

name: Rust slice::sort_by (LangArena Compress::BWTEncode) vs C++ std::sort and C radix prefix doubling
baseline: C++ version of the same test (prefix-doubling suffix array with std::sort and a pair-lookup comparator, g++ and clang++) and C version (LSD radix passes per doubling step)
workload: LangArena Compress::BWTEncode: Burrows-Wheeler transform of 100,000 generated bytes via prefix-doubling suffix sorting; 30 iterations (run.js).
claimed_speedup: Rust 0.422 s vs C/Gcc/Fast 0.699 s (best of all C/C++ configurations), C/Gcc 0.725 s, C++/G++/Fast 1.056 s, C++/G++ 1.179 s, C++/Clang++ 1.259 s. About 1.7x faster than the best C/C++ configuration and 2.5x faster than the best C++ configuration (derived from page data). Rust/PGO 0.413 s.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ 'prod' build: make -j prod with -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 (clang 22.1.8, g++ 16.0.1 20260322 trunk). Same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops, thin LTO), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, full LTO) and PGO variants of every C and C++ test; all of them are in the results file. Rust 1.99.0 (2026-09-28): cargo build --release (opt-level 3, no LTO).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (host kostya-ms7c37, results dated 2026-10-05)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Unverified inference from the sources: the Rust (sort_by on a Vec) and C++ (std::sort with a lambda) versions run the same prefix-doubling loop with a comparison sort over a suffix array that is already ordered by the previous round's ranks, so an adaptive stable sort that exploits existing runs (the Rust std stable sort) has less work than introsort; the C version replaces the comparison sort with radix passes (different algorithm).
stars_or_usage: 119.7k stars (rust-lang/rust); the benchmark suite has 41 stars
tradeoffs: The Rust pairs are (usize, usize) (16 bytes) versus (int32, int32) pairs in C++; memory 7.9 MB vs 8.1 MB for C++/G++.
caveats: Same underlying Rust std sort as the Sort::Self row, so it is not an independent second reason. Comparison sorts with indirect key lookups are cache-bound, so results may move with data size (100,000 bytes here). The Zig row (1.006 s) and Nim rows (0.854 s default) do not beat the best C row at default builds. Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kostya/LangArena/HEAD/cpp/src/compress.cpp, rust/src/benchmarks/compress.rs and c/src/compress.c. LangArena describes itself as a subjective benchmark; the README says AI tools assisted translating tests between languages and that idiomatic constructs are used per language. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance reported), single machine, one monthly run. Rows were selected by this agent as tests where the language beats every C/C++ configuration; most other tests in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): kostya/LangArena results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js, scanned for tests where a Rust, Zig, Nim, D, Odin, C3, V, Crystal or Swift row beats every non-instrumented C and C++ configuration; the C, C++ and language sources were then read to confirm the work is the same.
